summary: Step 7's SHIPPED PRODUCTION CODE is sound: I re-verified the lock's ordering (semantic_interpretation.py:403-416 registers the RunState only after a successful acquire and the release clears the slot before lock.release()), the release path (Connection.close() at rpc.py:241-254 is idempotent, runs every on_close callback once with a per-callback except/logger.exception, then closes the writer; handle_client's finally reaches it at :398-401), the ML bubble (semantic_store.ML:2287-2303: finaliser armed before the connection exists, connect-and-record uninterruptible with get_connection kept interruptible through `run`, the connection CLOSED and never released to the pool), all four NONE sites, `dry_run` left unwrapped, `interpret_with_parallel'` absent from SEMANTIC_STORE with exactly one caller, and the three §12 texts byte-exact against the plan (my own SML-literal parser, honouring the `\...\` gaps, matched plan lines 792/794/796 character for character). The suite reproduces the scope's baseline exactly (399 passed, 16 failed, all pre-existing). Ten of the eleven derivations are right as made; derivation 1 (module-level `_locked_run`) is not merely acceptable but load-bearing, because the run's consumers (interpret_file, the §5.6 startup check) run on pooled worker connections, not on the lock connection — the plan's §8.1 sentence is what is wrong, not the code. Step 7 is nevertheless NOT acceptable as it stands, for defects confined to the two test files, three comment/plan lines and two small ML shape changes: (a) the ML test's block 3 hangs forever instead of failing whenever the holder thread does not reach the lock body — `Synchronized.guarded_access` (synchronized.ML:89 → an unbounded `Thread.ConditionVar.wait`) waits on a flag written only inside the lock body, the session declares no timeout, and I confirmed a race-free path into it (try_acquire_cmd has `timeout = NONE`, semantic_store.ML:2279, which call_command' pushes into an indefinite `Socket.select`, RPC.ML:571/110-117); (b) the same theory calls the real `Semantic_Store.interpret` at :33 before checking, at :36, that the nested acquire was refused, so under the very regression the test guards it starts a live cone run (LLM spend on a scratch DB, gate writes into the real DB in a batch build) instead of aborting; (c) the theory is listed in Test/ROOT:20 while its own header (:6-9) says "Run through the REPL server only" with a scratch SEMANTIC_DB_DIR — the build satisfies neither (etc/settings sets no SEMANTIC_DB_DIR; paths.py:41-45 falls back to the user's real cache); (d) the Python suite does not pin the one invariant that makes derivation 1 sound — I reproduced this myself: moving `run = RunState(); _locked_run = run` above the acquire still passes 7/7, while the implementer's own control mutation fails 2; (e) §8.1's ownership sentence and §8.2's "the `fn run =>` form ... is new here" are both false of the code (schedule_dag shipped `uninterruptible_body` at semantic_store.ML:1969 in aa5b93c, and `\<^try>…finally` is itself built from it, isabelle_thread.ML:185-187). Two findings (the eager snapshot_sync import, the tests' repository) are refuted on measurement and rejected; the process-risk "finding" restates a CLAUDE.md rule that aa5b93c already follows, and its one live question is passed to the user. I also accept, with reason, the implementer's disclosed §10 deviation that the callback arm's §12 #1 writeln and the collect app's §12 #3 error are not driven by a test: both arms are straight-line ML, their texts are byte-verified, and driving them needs a Python caller holding the lock / the REPL app protocol.

rulings.title: The ML test hangs forever (instead of failing) whenever the holder thread does not get the lock
rulings.rationale: Verified on the distribution source, not inferred: `fun guarded_access var f = the (timed_access var (fn _ => NONE) f)` (Isabelle2025-2/src/Pure/Concurrent/synchronized.ML:89) and, with no time limit, `NONE => (Thread.ConditionVar.wait (cond, lock); Exn.Res true)` (multithreading.ML:67) — an unbounded, un-polled wait. `started` is written only inside the lock body (Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:55), so refusal (`Exn.Res NONE`), a raise, or a fork stuck in the acquire all park the main thread at :63 with the answer already sitting unread in `outcome` (:58-62). There is no outer bound: Test/ROOT declares no `timeout` for the session, so with the theory in the build (Test/ROOT:20) this is a wedged build job rather than a red test, which violates the project's own 'monitor long-running tasks' discipline and destroys the signal the test exists to give. I accept the rebuttal's refutation of evidence path (a): a persistently held foreign lock fails earlier, at :20, so that path collapses into the narrow release/acquire race. But I independently confirmed a second path that needs no race at all: `try_acquire_cmd` is declared `timeout = NONE` (semantic_store.ML:2279), `call_command'` pushes that straight onto the socket (`val _ = (#3 conn) := timeout`, Isabelle_RPC/Tools/RPC.ML:571), and the read is `Socket.select {... timeout = !read_timeout}` (RPC.ML:110-117), which blocks indefinitely on NONE — so a host that degrades after the theory's earlier blocks succeeded parks the fork inside the acquire with `started` still false. The rebuttal is also right that the `\<^try>…finally` half of the original fix is redundant (`Exn.capture` at :53 already runs on every path); the variable that is not written unconditionally is the wake-up signal, and only that. Severity major rather than minor because the failure mode is an unbounded hang in the project's regression command, not a wrong answer; the production code is untouched by this. fix-then-rereview because the fix restructures block 3 and the characteristic way to get it wrong (recomputing the deadline inside `time_limit`, which `timed_access` re-evaluates on every wakeup) is invisible except by reading the new code against a REPL run.
rulings.fix: Collapse `started` and `outcome` (Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:44-45) into ONE state variable so that 'the main thread can be woken only by a state the holder can reach' becomes structural: `datatype holder_state = Not_started | Holding | Done of string`, set to `Holding` inside the lock body and to `Done msg` after `Exn.capture` returns, with `Exn.Res (SOME ())` reported as "finished", `Exn.Res NONE` as "refused" (today :60 conflates the two) and `Exn.Exn` as "interrupted"/"failed". Replace the `guarded_access` at :63 with `Synchronized.timed_access` whose predicate returns on ANY terminal state (`fn Not_started => NONE | s => SOME (s, s)`) and asserts `= SOME Holding`, so a refused or failed acquire fails the assertion at once instead of stalling to the deadline. Compute the deadline ONCE, outside, and pass it as `K (SOME deadline)`: `timed_access` evaluates `time_limit x` on each retry (synchronized.ML:75), so an inline `Time.now () + …` would renew the bound on every spurious wakeup. Use a second `timed_access` on the same variable to replace `Isabelle_Thread.join` + the post-hoc `Time.now () - t0 < 10 s` check (:67-69), turning 'released within 10 s' into the success condition of a bounded wait rather than an assertion only reached if an unbounded join happens to return; keep the `join` afterwards as tidy-up. Then run the theory through the REPL server and hand the transcript to the re-review. (Not required here, and a new decision if wanted: giving `try_acquire_cmd` a finite `timeout` the way `heartbeat_cmd` has one, RPC.ML:586, would close the wedged-host path in production too — but every long RPC in this file is `timeout = NONE` by design, so that is not step 7's business.)

rulings.title: The ML test calls the real `Semantic_Store.interpret` without first checking that the nested acquire was refused
rulings.rationale: Literally true on disk: `nested` is bound at Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:31, `Semantic_Store.interpret false (Context.Proof \<^context>)` runs unconditionally at :33, and `nested` is first inspected at :36, after the whole body has returned. Nothing between :31 and :33 looks at it. The guard on that call is therefore the very mechanism under test: `fun interpret force context = (case interpret_with_parallel context force [context] of SOME () => () | NONE => error lock_busy_error)` (semantic_store.ML:2404-2407) reaches its `error` arm only because the nested acquire is refused, so a lock that wrongly grants re-entry sends :33 into `interpret_with_parallel'` (:2333) — collect_cone over the ancestor cone of Semantic_Embedding.Semantic_Embedding, check_embedding_service, interpret_cone with the configured driver. The cone is essentially all of HOL: `is_excluded_theory` excludes only Code_Generator, Pure, Code_Evaluation and Typerep (:397-400, :1922-1923). The two harms are environment-split, and I would state them that way rather than with an 'and': with the scratch SEMANTIC_DB_DIR the header prescribes, nothing is pre-interpreted so the run is the full cone and maximal LLM spend; with the real cache (which is exactly what a batch build gets — see agreement-S7-01) most theories are skipped but any due entity is interpreted and gate-written into the user's real database from a test. The probe is also a faithful predictor of the dangerous call: `_try_acquire_interpretation_lock` returns on `_LockTimeout` before creating the RunState or touching `connection.on_close` (semantic_interpretation.py:403-416), so a refused probe leaves no residue and both go through the same `with_interpretation_lock`. This is the project's own elegance rule at its sharpest — establish a fact, then act on it, not the reverse — and the fix is one line that turns a money-and-data regression into an immediate abort. Contingent on a lock regression, yes; but that regression is precisely what this theory exists to catch, so it is not a hypothetical.
rulings.fix: Check inside the body, before the live entry point, and let the body return only the error text (the tuple has no reason to exist once `nested` is checked where it is established). In Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:27-38: inside `with_interpretation_lock`, first `if Semantic_Store.with_interpretation_lock (fn () => ()) = NONE then () else error "interpretation lock broken: a nested acquire succeeded -- refusing to start a live interpretation run"`, then the existing `(Semantic_Store.interpret false (Context.Proof \<^context>); NONE) handle ERROR msg => SOME msg`, and simplify :36 to `\<^assert> (r = SOME (SOME Semantic_Store.lock_busy_error))`. Use `error`, not `\<^assert>`: `\<^assert>` raises only `General.Fail "Assertion failed"` (ml_antiquotations.ML:22-23), and this is the one abort whose job is to say why the run was refused. The raise happens inside the outer holder's body, so `with_interpretation_lock`'s `\<^try>\<open>… finally …\<close>` (semantic_store.ML:2291-2302) still closes the connection and frees the lock. The header's claim at :6 that the theory 'never runs an interpretation' then holds by construction instead of by trust.

rulings.title: The acquire's slot-ordering invariant is not pinned by any test: a mutation that registers the RunState before the acquire succeeds passes all 7
rulings.rationale: I reproduced this myself rather than taking either side's word, with a positive control, using pytest plugins that only rebind `SI._try_acquire_interpretation_lock` (no repo file touched, plugin dir outside the repo). Baseline: 7 passed. Control mutation from the implementer's own list ('run state not registered'): 2 failed, 5 passed — so the mechanism bites. Ordering mutation (`run = RunState(); _locked_run = run` moved above `try: lock.acquire()`, nothing else changed): 7 passed. The invariant is unguarded, and it is the one that makes derivation 1 sound: a refused acquirer must not touch the holder's slot. It is reachable without any exotic topology — `get_connection` hands out pooled connections against the one per-session host (RPC.ML:880-910), so a nested refusal arrives at the very host process holding the lock, which is exactly what Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:31 and :64 drive; under the mutation that refusal overwrites `_locked_run`, the holder's `release` then finds `_locked_run is run` false (semantic_interpretation.py:411) and never clears the slot, and `current_run_state()` keeps handing a dead run's `prefilter_disabled` to later callers. The shipped ordering (:403-406 returning before :407/:416) is correct; this is test hardening, and the scope puts the test file and the mutation list (SCOPE.md:65-66, :122-125) under review. Minor, as claimed — not more.
rulings.fix: Put the invariant in the `_acquire` helper (archive/tests/test_interpretation_lock.py:46-51) rather than in one test body, so every refusal in the file is pinned by construction — the helper already carries the other per-refusal invariant (D8's 'back within 0.5 s'): capture `held = SI._locked_run` before the call and, `if not got: assert SI._locked_run is held`. I measured both candidates: the helper form leaves the shipped code at 7 passed and makes the ordering mutant fail TWO tests (test_two_instances_in_one_process_exclude_each_other_until_the_holder_closes and test_two_processes_on_one_directory_exclude_each_other), i.e. it also covers the cross-process refusal at :127 that an in-test assertion would miss. Drop the finding's optional `assert SI._locked_run is None` after `a.close()`: :73 already asserts exactly that. Add a seventh entry to the mutation list in the step's record: 'the RunState registered before the acquire instead of after'.

rulings.title: Interpretation_Lock_Test is in Test/ROOT, but its own header says it must not be run that way
rulings.rationale: The contradiction is real and is step 7's own doing: `Interpretation_Lock_Test` is absent from `git show aa5b93c:Test/ROOT` and present at Test/ROOT:20 today, while the theory header (:6-9) says 'start that server with SEMANTIC_DB_DIR pointing at a scratch directory. Run through the REPL server only.' A batch build satisfies neither: contrib/Semantic_Embedding/etc/settings sets no SEMANTIC_DB_DIR (I read the whole file — it sets only ISABELLE_SEMANTIC_EMBEDDING_HOME and a classpath), and paths.py:41-45 then falls back to `platformdirs.user_cache_dir("Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding", "Qiyuan")`. One of the two texts must go. I take the rebuttal's direction over the finding's, on three verified grounds: the session is meant to be built (Interpretation_Driver_Config_Test.thy:14 'A build failure here = a regression'), §10 explicitly asks for this ML test, and the session already declares the discipline this theory needs — Test_All.thy:163-169 says 'never run it concurrently with a live interpretation' and errors out in exactly that case. The severity is minor, not major: Test/ROOT:1-11 keeps the session out of the top-level ROOT so no end user's build reaches it; the acquire's only filesystem effect is `os.makedirs(exist_ok=True)` plus the `.interpretation.lock` file filelock deletes on release (semantic_interpretation.py:399-402); and every locked body in the theory is trivial, with :33 short-circuiting at semantic_store.ML:2405-2407. The residual effects are a spurious build failure if a live run holds the lock, and a concurrent auto-update skipped with §12 #1 for the seconds the theory holds it. NB this finding and ml-S7-ML-2 compound: with the ROOT line kept, a lock regression would make a routine `isabelle build -d . -d Test` write interpretations into the real database — which is why ML-2's one-line guard must land with this.
rulings.fix: Keep Test/ROOT:20. Rewrite the theory header's two false sentences (Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:6-9) to state what is true and load-bearing: the theory takes the interpretation lock briefly and writes NOTHING to the database (every locked body is trivial and `interpret` short-circuits at semantic_store.ML:2405-2407; the `.interpretation.lock` file, deleted on release, is its only artefact), so it is safe under whatever SEMANTIC_DB_DIR the attached host has; like its sibling Test_All.thy:163-165 it follows the session's test-exclusivity discipline — do not build this session while a live interpretation is running, or :20 fails spuriously, and in the other direction a concurrent auto-update is skipped with §12 #1 while the theory holds the lock; pointing SEMANTIC_DB_DIR at a scratch directory (how it was developed) removes even that coupling. If the user instead wants the 'REPL-only' rule to stand, the ROOT line must go — but then §10's lock test never runs under the project's regression command, which is the worse trade; that call is listed for the user.

rulings.title: §8.1's ownership sentence does not describe the code
rulings.rationale: The literal phrase at plan §8.1 (line 600) — 'stores the FileLock and the run's `RunState` (§15.8) on the `Connection`' — is not what the code does: nothing is set as an attribute of `Connection`; one `release` closure holding both is appended to `connection.on_close` (semantic_interpretation.py:415) and the `RunState` is additionally published in the module-level slot `_locked_run` (:379, :416), which §8.1 never mentions. The plan and the code must agree, so §8.1 gets a one-sentence refresh. I reject the finding's strongest claim, 'the RunState half cannot be done as written': the rebuttal demonstrated a working attribute-on-Connection form with a module-level pointer, so the case for the closure is elegance (one global instead of a global plus two untyped attributes plus a dereference, and a release that structurally gives back exactly what its acquire took), not feasibility — and derivation 1 is right on that ground. I also reject the demand to rewrite §15.8: lines 1427-1433 say the acquire creates the RunState, the connection's `on_close` releases it, and 'a module-level `current_run_state()` accessor is per run by construction', which is precisely the implementation; its premise holds too, since `semantic_DB_dir()` is process-level (Isabelle_RPC/Isabelle_RPC_Host/paths.py:41-45), never per-connection. No code change; minor, documentation only.
rulings.fix: Edit plan §8.1 by hand (no scripted edit): replace 'stores the FileLock and the run's `RunState` (§15.8) on the `Connection`' with a sentence saying that the procedure appends to the acquiring `Connection`'s `on_close` one `release` closure holding the FileLock and the run's `RunState` (§15.8), and only then publishes the `RunState` in the module-level slot `_locked_run` that `current_run_state()` reads; the closure clears the slot (if it still holds this run) and releases the lock; nothing is set as an attribute of the connection — the closure IS the ownership; the slot is needed because the run state's consumers (`interpret_file`, the §5.6 startup check) run on OTHER, pooled connections while the lock connection carries nothing but the acquire. Leave §15.8 untouched.

rulings.title: The lock-name import makes semantic_interpretation the first eager importer of snapshot_sync
rulings.rationale: The bare fact is true and everything built on it is false. There is no 'lazy-import discipline' to break: every function-local import the finding cites is a CYCLE BREAKER — I confirmed that snapshot_sync imports `semantics`, `semantic_embedding` and `experience_index` back at function level (snapshot_sync.py:290, 381, 711, 757, 791-793, 958, 1002, 1014, 1016), so a top-level import at those sites would be an ImportError, not a slower start — while `grep -n semantic_interpretation snapshot_sync.py` returns exactly one hit, a comment at :243. There is no cycle to break here, so the plain top-level import at semantic_interpretation.py:48 is the ordinary shape, matching the seven other package-sibling imports at :30-47, and hiding it inside the acquire would make the acquire path's dependency invisible at the top of the file — worse by the elegance criterion, not better. The cost claim is also wrong: I measured `import Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding` on this machine at 0.90 s with 890 modules, of which zstandard, lmdb, platformdirs and diskcache were already present before step 7 (semantic_interpretation.py:40 has imported semantic_embedding since before this step); snapshot_sync plus tarfile is a low-single-digit-millisecond delta. And the proposed fix does not even achieve its stated goal, since `filelock` is eager through semantic_interpretation.py:24, which the fix leaves alone. The only true residue — conda/recipe.yaml:403-405's comment is measurably wrong in several names — was already wrong before step 7 and lives in a file that is not in the step-7 diff at all (the diff touches 8 files: semantic_interpretation.py, snapshot_sync.py, Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy, Test/ROOT, interpret_command.ML, semantic_interpretation_app.ML, semantic_store.ML, test_interpretation_lock.py). Hand that to whoever owns packaging; it is not a step-7 finding, and under the scope's rules this is a hypothetical with no concrete failure.
rulings.fix: No change. Do not touch semantic_interpretation.py:48.

rulings.title: `interpret_with_parallel'` is a top-level unlocked live-run entry whose only guard is a prime
rulings.rationale: The structural half stands and I verified it: `fun interpret_with_parallel' …` at semantic_store.ML:2333 is a top-level, unlocked live-run entry; a repo-wide grep finds exactly two occurrences of the name (:2333 and :2396), i.e. one caller; and the comment that carries the invariant ('Every live run goes through the lock; a dry run never does (D8)', :2394) sits on the wrapper rather than on the thing that must not be called. The fix is not exotic in this file: `local … in … end` is already used for exactly this hiding purpose at :415-448 and :597-616. Under the project rule the scope quotes verbatim, a three-line change that removes a name carrying a safety invariant is worth making. I reject the naming half of the finding outright: measured against this file rather than RPC.ML, the prime consistently means 'the same operation minus an outer layer' (`is_interpreted'` :360, `mark_interpreted'` :367, `interpret'` :1887, `dry_run'` :1909 with its signature gloss 'Level 2 alone, one theory, no level-1 due-filter'), so `interpret_with_parallel'` is on-convention and a rename to `…_unlocked` would be the inconsistency. I also correct the exposure figure: ML scoping is sequential, the structure runs :238-2565, so the unlocked name is visible to ~230 lines, not ~2500, and `dry_run` (:2215-2271) is defined before it and cannot reach it; the one live-run call site inside that window, :2451, already goes through the locked wrapper. Minor, on the structural argument alone.
rulings.fix: Either wrap the body in `local fun interpret_with_parallel' … in (* Every live run goes through the lock; a dry run never does (D8). *) fun interpret_with_parallel cfg_context force roots = with_interpretation_lock (fn () => interpret_with_parallel' cfg_context force roots) end` — the idiom this file already uses twice, and the minimal diff — or inline the ~60-line body directly into the lock's body and delete the second name entirely, which is stronger (the unlocked entry becomes nameless) at the cost of re-indenting. Do NOT rename to `…_unlocked`.

rulings.title: `uninterruptible` with a dummy unit argument where `uninterruptible_body` is the exact idiom — in both the code and §8.2's block
rulings.rationale: Verified end to end. The two functions are declared side by side (Isabelle2025-2/src/Pure/Concurrent/thread_attributes.ML:20-21, identical in Isabelle2024), and the short form is definitionally the long one: `fun uninterruptible_body body = uninterruptible (fn run => fn () => body run) ();` (thread_attributes.ML:110-111). So semantic_store.ML:2293-2295 hand-inlines the definition of a function it could call, and the interruptible-through-`run` property the comment at :2281-2286 depends on is preserved exactly. This is not taste but an in-file inconsistency: the SAME file already uses `Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible_body (fn run => …)` in `schedule_dag` at :1969, and that line is already committed (`git show aa5b93c:Tools/semantic_store.ML` → line 1961). Worse, the expression sits two lines below a `\<^try>\<open>… finally …\<close>` which expands to `Isabelle_Thread.try_finally`, itself built from `uninterruptible_body` (isabelle_thread.ML:185-187). That makes the plan's prose at §8.2 lines 625-627 — 'the `fn run =>` form … is new here' — factually false about this codebase, which is a concrete plan/code disagreement and admissible on its own. I note explicitly that this is NOT an implementer slip: semantic_store.ML:2293-2295 reproduces the approved §8.2 block character for character (plan lines 634-635); the defect originates in the plan and the code inherited it, so both must move together. No behavioural difference, hence minor.
rulings.fix: Code: in semantic_store.ML:2293-2295 replace `Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible (fn run => fn () => let val c = run Remote_Procedure_Calling.get_connection () in conn := SOME c; c end) ()` with `Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible_body (fn run => let val c = run Remote_Procedure_Calling.get_connection () in conn := SOME c; c end)`. The comment at :2281-2286 already speaks in terms of `run` and needs no change. Plan: mirror the same change in the §8.2 code block (lines 634-635) and replace the false prose with a true one naming `uninterruptible_body` (thread_attributes.ML:21), `schedule_dag` (semantic_store.ML:1969) and `Isabelle_Thread.try_finally` (isabelle_thread.ML:186) as the precedents — by hand, no scripted edit. The two `uninterruptible (fn _ => fn () => …) ()` sites in Isabelle_RPC/Tools/RPC.ML (:814, :838) would take the same simplification but sit inside another agent's uncommitted work; leave them.

rulings.title: Isabelle_RPC's `Connection.close()` contract is tested only in Semantic_Embedding (derivation 9)
rulings.rationale: The premise 'Isabelle_RPC has its own standalone pytest files, so there was a home for them' is false, and I checked it directly: contrib/Isabelle_RPC has no conftest.py and no pytest configuration in pyproject.toml, and its `test_callback.py` / `test_multiplexed.py` define `async def test_*(arg, connection)` decorated with `@isabelle_remote_procedure` — Isabelle-side remote procedures served to test_callback.ML, which pytest would collect and error on. Its only workflow, .github/workflows/release-conda.yml, is triggered by workflow_dispatch and `push: tags: ['v*']`, and its pytest invocations are exactly `python -m pytest test_attached_host.py -v` (lines 309 and 466). A new test_connection_close.py dropped beside test_protocol_standalone.py would be executed by nothing. Meanwhile the tests' current home is the suite that actually runs (399 passing), and `Isabelle_RPC_Host.rpc` resolves to the working tree, so those two tests today guard the very file another agent is editing. Moving them would create the exact regression window the finding warns about. The docstring at archive/tests/test_interpretation_lock.py:7-9 states and justifies the placement; derivation 9 stands. The finding's evidence also misattributes rpc.py:242-254 to the other agent — those lines ARE step 7's `close()`. The substantive cross-repo concern is not the directory but the version floor, which I raise separately for the user.
rulings.fix: No change. Leave the two `Connection.close()` tests where they are.

rulings.title: The two-process test's second half is not cross-process, though its comment says it is
rulings.rationale: The mechanical claim is true: `_hold_in_child` returns right after `hold.send("released")` (test_interpretation_lock.py:101-107), the parent consumed that at :129, and nothing is sent to the child afterwards (the only later contact is `proc.terminate()` at :136), so the `with pytest.raises(Timeout): FileLock(path, timeout=0).acquire()` at :132-133 runs in the test process itself — same-process exclusion, which :54-61 already establishes. The comment 'and the other way round: while we hold it, a plain FileLock elsewhere fails', inside a test named test_two_processes_on_one_directory_exclude_each_other and directly after a genuine cross-process exchange, claims more than the code checks; a test asserting less than its comment says is a small correctness defect, not merely a comment nit. I reject the coverage claim built on it: plan line 745 asks for two items — 'two processes on one `SEMANTIC_DB_DIR`; two instances in one process' — and both are driven (:120-129 and :54-61); §8.3 decomposes flock by HALVES (cross-process vs same-instance), never by direction, and flock exclusion is one kernel-level mutual exclusion with no independently-failable second direction. I also endorse the rebuttal's warning that the finding's preferred fix would hang: `_holder_process` (:113-117) keeps the parent's copy of the `child` pipe end alive through the Process object's args, so a later `parent.recv()` after the child has exited never sees EOF and blocks forever — turning a test failure into a wedged suite, the very thing derivation 7 was written to prevent.
rulings.fix: Cheapest honest edit: delete :131-133; the test then covers exactly the plan's 'two processes on one SEMANTIC_DB_DIR' and nothing else. If the line is kept as an at-a-glance check, make the comment say what it is (e.g. 'and symmetrically, here in the test process: while we hold it a plain FileLock is refused'), dropping 'the other way round' and 'elsewhere'. Correct the same wording in the step's handoff record, ai-artifacts/review_step7/SCOPE.md:104 ('both directions'). If the genuinely cross-process direction is wanted, it needs three changes together, not one: `_hold_in_child` must stay alive for a further 'try' message and answer 'refused'/'got it'; `_holder_process` must `child.close()` after `proc.start()` so a dead child yields EOFError; and every `parent.recv()` must be guarded by `parent.poll(5)`.

rulings.title: Comments left describing step 7 as still in the future
rulings.rationale: Confirmed for the Python half only. `RunState`'s class docstring (semantic_interpretation.py:356-359) still reads 'one holder of the interpretation lock (§8, §13 step 7) once the lock lands; until then, one `interpret_file`', and 'once the lock lands' is implementation-time, not runtime: it condenses plan §15.8's 'until the lock lands (§13 step 7) no run ever holds one, so steps 3-6 run entirely on the off-lock scope', whose consequent talks about implementation steps. What makes it more than a stale comment is that the same diff deleted exactly this sentence four lines below — working_tree.diff:38-42 shows `current_run_state`'s 'No run holds the lock before §13 step 7' being replaced — so the file now contradicts itself four lines apart, and it is the docstring on the class that names the concept which is wrong. I reject the ML half: semantic_store.ML:2310-2311 says '(the flag reaches the run's theories once the lock creates the run's state, §13 step 7)', a conditional that is true of the shipped code (the lock does create the RunState, semantic_interpretation.py:407) with a plan pointer attached, and `with_interpretation_lock` is defined nineteen lines above it at :2287, so a reader meets the landed lock first. I also reject the §15.8 edit: that sentence is the plan's correct record of why steps 3-6 could be built and reviewed before the lock existed, and churning approved plan prose for no gain is not worth it.
rulings.fix: One edit, one file. Replace semantic_interpretation.py:356-359 with a timeless statement that agrees with `current_run_state`'s docstring and points at it rather than restating its rule, e.g. 'State scoped to one interpretation run (plan §15.8 "Run-scoped state"): the holder of the interpretation lock (§8); off the lock, one `interpret_file` (`current_run_state`).' Leave Tools/semantic_store.ML:2310-2311 and plan §15.8 exactly as they are.

rulings.title: PROCESS RISK: step 7 cannot be committed without sweeping in another agent's uncommitted interrupt work
rulings.rationale: Rejected as a review finding; its one live question is carried to the user's list instead, as the judging brief asks. Every element is either pre-authorised, already practised, or carved out of this review. CLAUDE.md's 'Commit on `main` — never branch' says verbatim that another agent's swept-in changes are acceptable provided the commit message describes their work — and the finding's own fix quotes that rule, so the remedy is 'do what the rule already says'. The implementer is already doing it: `git log -1 aa5b93c` ends with 'Also sweeps in another agent's two uncommitted lines in semantic_store.ML (`on_interrupt = Remote_Procedure_Calling.Reraise` …)'. SCOPE.md:36-41 explicitly says 'Do not review the rest', and the finding's evidence section is 'the rest'. Its one genuinely new fact — Semantic_Embedding@aa5b93c does not compile against Isabelle_RPC@65cdbaa because `on_interrupt` exists only in the uncommitted tree, which I confirmed (`git show aa5b93c:Tools/semantic_store.ML | grep on_interrupt` → :398, :2359; `git show HEAD:Tools/RPC.ML | grep on_interrupt` → nothing) — the finding itself concedes predates step 7, and it was introduced under step 6's accepted, disclosed sweep. Step 7's own `close_connection` export (RPC.ML:58-61, consumed at semantic_store.ML:2302) is a different animal: it is the implementer's own code, so the lockstep it creates is one they control end to end. One factual error: Tools/pide_state.ML carries five `on_interrupt` insertions, not six (`git diff --stat` → 5; `grep -c` → 5).
rulings.fix: No code change. When step 7 lands, name the swept-in work in both commit messages exactly as aa5b93c did — on the Isabelle_RPC side the interrupt work (IsabelleInterrupt, the `error == "Interrupt"` arm, the on_interrupt datatype and mk_callback rewrite, plus the edits in Universal_Key/config/context/dialogue/theory_hash/tracing.ML), on the Semantic_Embedding side that agent's `on_interrupt = Remote_Procedure_Calling.Reraise` insertions in Tools/explain_term.ML (2) and Tools/pide_state.ML (5) and the temporary hunt marker at Tools/entity_position.ML:141-143. Ordering is forced, not a choice: the Isabelle_RPC commit must precede the parent repo's submodule bump, since step 7's ML calls `Remote_Procedure_Calling.close_connection`.

plan_edits: §8.1, line 600 (edit by hand, no scripted replace). CURRENT: "`Semantic_Store.try_acquire_interpretation_lock` → bool stores the FileLock and the run's `RunState` (§15.8) on the `Connection`". PROPOSED: "`Semantic_Store.try_acquire_interpretation_lock` → bool appends to the acquiring `Connection`'s `on_close` one `release` closure that holds the FileLock and the run's `RunState` (§15.8), and only then publishes the `RunState` in the module-level slot `_locked_run` that `current_run_state()` reads; the closure clears the slot (if it still holds this run) and releases the lock. Nothing is set as an attribute of the connection — the closure IS the ownership, so a release can only give back what its own acquire took. The slot is needed because the run state's consumers (`interpret_file`, the §5.6 startup check) run on OTHER connections — the pooled ones serving each theory — while the lock connection carries nothing but the acquire." The rest of the sentence (the `on_close` / `_closed` description) stays as it is.

§8.2, lines 625-627. CURRENT: "the `fn run =>` form, which keeps `get_connection ()` interruptible inside the bubble, is new here (`Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible` accepts it, thread_attributes.ML:20)". PROPOSED: "`Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible_body` (thread_attributes.ML:21) keeps `get_connection ()` interruptible inside the bubble through `run` — the same form `schedule_dag` already uses (semantic_store.ML:1969) and the one `Isabelle_Thread.try_finally`, i.e. `\\<^try>\\<open>… finally …\\<close>` itself, is built from (isabelle_thread.ML:186)". (The claim 'is new here' is false: schedule_dag shipped that form in aa5b93c.)

§8.2, code block lines 634-635. CURRENT: "        val c = Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible (fn run => fn () =>\n                  let val c = run get_connection () in conn := SOME c; c end) ()". PROPOSED: "        val c = Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible_body (fn run =>\n                  let val c = run get_connection () in conn := SOME c; c end)". The two forms are definitionally identical (thread_attributes.ML:110-111), so nothing else in the block or its prose changes.

OPTIONAL, citation hygiene in the same two subsections — replace rotting line numbers with site names, since these numbers were already stale before step 7 and today's tree is contaminated by another agent's uncommitted work. §8.1, line 603-604: "`handle_client`'s `finally`, rpc.py:374, and from `Connection.__aexit__`, :232" → "`handle_client`'s `finally` and `Connection.__aexit__`". §8.2, line 657: "semantics.py:1850, 1885" → "`update_interpretations`' two live `interpret_theories` callbacks" (they sit at :1873 and :1909 today, and were already at those lines at the step-6 commit; the dry call at :1865 is the only one whose result is unpacked). Do NOT re-pin these to today's numbers.
for_the_user: Which way to resolve the Test/ROOT vs theory-header contradiction (finding agreement-S7-01). My recommendation, and what I ruled: KEEP `Interpretation_Lock_Test` in Test/ROOT:20 and fix the header, because §10 asks for this ML test and `isabelle build -d . -d Test Semantic_Embedding_Test` is the project's regression command — a theory in no session is a theory nobody runs. The consequence you are being asked to accept is that this command briefly takes the interpretation lock on whatever SEMANTIC_DB_DIR the builder's environment has, which by default is your real cache (~/.cache/Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding): it writes nothing, but it fails spuriously if a live interpretation run is in progress, and for the few seconds it holds the lock a concurrent `by aoa` auto-update is skipped with §12 #1. The session already declares this discipline for a sibling theory (Test_All.thy:163-169). If you would rather the regression build never touch the real lock, the alternative is to drop the ROOT line and run this theory by hand through the REPL only — at the cost that §10's lock test is outside the regression gate.

The process question you asked me to surface: committing step 7's Isabelle_RPC change (`Connection.on_close` / `_closed` / `close()` in rpc.py, the `on_close` line in rpc.pyi, the `close_connection` signature entry in RPC.ML) beside another agent's uncommitted interrupt work. CLAUDE.md already pre-authorises the sweep provided the commit message names the other agent's work, and aa5b93c did exactly that, so no rule stands in the way — what remains is your call on sequencing: (a) wait for the interrupt work to land in Isabelle_RPC and commit step 7 on top, or (b) commit both together now with the sweep described. Two facts that bear on it: contrib/Isabelle_RPC's working tree carries eleven modified files, not just the three of step 7; and on the Semantic_Embedding side the sweep would also take that agent's `on_interrupt` insertions in Tools/explain_term.ML (2 lines) and Tools/pide_state.ML (5 lines) plus the self-declared TEMPORARY hunt marker at Tools/entity_position.ML:141-143 ('Delete with the hunt'). Ordering within the choice is forced either way: the Isabelle_RPC commit must land before the parent repo's submodule pointer is bumped, because step 7's ML calls `Remote_Procedure_Calling.close_connection`.

A packaging decision raised during rebuttal, not in the original findings, that step 7 makes live: `Connection.on_close` is an UNRELEASED Isabelle_RPC feature, but contrib/Isabelle_RPC/VERSION already reads 0.5.0 (committed in 327ca4c, no v0.5.0 tag cut yet) while contrib/Semantic_Embedding/pyproject.toml:60 pins `isabelle-rpc>=0.5.0`. If a v0.5.0 is tagged before `on_close` is committed, a conda install satisfies the floor and then AttributeErrors at semantic_interpretation.py:415 the first time a run takes the lock. Decide one of: bump VERSION to 0.5.1 with `on_close` and raise the floor to it, or simply never cut v0.5.0 until `on_close` is in. Either way the pyproject comment at :49-59, which already spells out two reasons for the 0.5.0 floor, should gain `Connection.on_close` as the third.
